content:
Humans have valued mushrooms as food since antiquity. The delineation between edible and poisonous fungi is unclear. As a result, a "mushroom" may be edible, poisonous, or unpalatable. The terms "mushroom" and "toadstool" go back centuries. The term "mushroom" may have been derived from the French word “mousseron,” meaning moss (mousse). The word toadstool appeared first in 14th-century England. These terms likely implied their toxic nature. Many species of mushrooms seemingly appear overnight, growing rapidly. This phenomenon is the source of several common sayings in English, including "to mushroom" (expand rapidly in size or scope) and "to pop up like a mushroom" (to appear quickly out of the blue). Not all mushrooms expand from one day to the next. Some grow very slowly and add tissue by growing from the colony’s edges. For example, Pleurotus nebrodensis grows slowly. Because of this and humans harvesting it, the species is now critically endangered.

Mushrooms are fungi. The field of biology that studies fungi is known as mycology. Scientists study how fungi are vital for life on earth in their roles as symbionts, meaning that fungi depend on other beings for survival. A fungus is eukaryotic because it has cells with a nucleus. This group includes plants, animals, yeasts, molds, and mushrooms. But fungi are classified in their own kingdom. That means mushrooms are neither plants nor animals. Fungi, like animals, are heterotrophs. That is an organism that cannot produce its own food, instead taking nutrition from other sources of organic carbon, like plant or animal matter. In the food chain, heterotrophs are primary, secondary, and tertiary consumers, but not producers. Fungi do not photosynthesize, so unlike producers, they cannot make energy from the sun. Fungi are the main decomposers in ecological systems. By decomposing this matter, fungi play a critical role in the global carbon cycle.

Mycelium (plural mycelia) is a root-like structure of a fungus made of a mass of thread-like hyphae that branch out. Fungal colonies of mycelium are found in and on soil and many other substrates. A substrate is a surface on which an organism (such as a plant, fungus, or animal) lives. For example, algae live on a rock; the rock is the substrate. Through the mycelium, a fungus absorbs nutrients. It does this in a two-stage process. First, the hyphae secrete enzymes into the food source to break it down. Nutrients are then absorbed into the mycelium. Mycelia are vital in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems for their role in the decomposition of plant material. They contribute to the organic fraction of soil. They are vital to agriculture and are important to almost all species of plants, as mycelia are a primary factor in a plant's health, nutrient intake, and growth.

Armillaria ostoyae is common in cooler regions of the northern hemisphere. This fungus is found on coniferous trees in the Pacific Northwest forests and parts of Asia. One was found in the Malheur National Forest in the Strawberry Mountains in Oregon and is the largest fungal colony in the world. It spans an area of 3.5 square miles (2,200 acres). This organism is thought to be some 8,000 years old and may weigh as much as 35,000 tons. If this colony is understood as a single organism, it is one of the largest known organisms in the world by area. It is only rivaled by a seaweed colony of Posidonia australis in Australia that measures 48 square miles (49,000 acres). Another "humongous fungus" is Armillaria gallica. One in Michigan covers 0.142 square miles (91 acres) and originated from a parent fungus in Canada.
